Usage: python -m pynakes ref show [OPTIONS] [file] [key]

  Show one uniquely identified reference, or triage several at once.

  With a citation key this prints every stored field of that one reference.
  With `--key k1,k2,...` it prints a compact summary of each requested
  reference instead — title, creator, date, venue, and identifiers, plus the
  abstract under `--abstract` — so a set of candidates can be scanned in one
  call rather than one invocation per key. Both forms refuse to guess when a
  key is duplicated, and the `--key` form reports every unknown key together.
  `--where EXPR` summarizes every entry the selector matches, in file order —
  `--where 'query "to-read"'` runs a saved query, and `used`/`unused` test the
  bibliography's linked TeX sources.

  Bounded reads: `--select` returns only the named fields (the abstract among
  them); `--include materials,provenance` adds the materials available for
  each entry and the provenance the bibliography recorded; `--max-chars` cuts
  long values and lists every cut under `truncated`. With `--key` or
  `--where`, `--limit` pages the selection and `page.next_cursor` resumes it —

answer.text:
# Abstracts in the group "Optics" (12 entries)

The group has 12 entries. I read them in three pages of at most 5 entries each, with every value cut to 300 characters. Every abstract was longer than that (774 to 789 characters), so each summary below covers only its first 300 characters. In every entry those 300 characters hold one sentence, repeated. That sentence has the same pattern throughout: "We describe the <X> apparatus in detail, report measurements of its behaviour under controlled illumination, and compare them with the classical account."

Each abstract describes an optical apparatus in detail, reports measurements of how it behaves under controlled illumination, and compares those measurements with the classical account. The only difference between abstracts is the apparatus studied.

| Key | Title | Apparatus | Abstract length |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ashby1950 | On the Lens Problem, Part 1 | lens | 774 |
| Gisler1952 | On the Mirror Problem, Part 3 | mirror | 784 |
| Elling1954 | On the Fibre Problem, Part 5 | fibre | 779 |
| Castell1956 | On the Crystal Problem, Part 7 | crystal | 789 |
| Ashby1958 | On the Lens Problem, Part 9 | lens | 774 |
| Gisler1960 | On the Mirror Problem, Part 11 | mirror | 784 |
| Elling1962 | On the Fibre Problem, Part 13 | fibre | 779 |
| Castell1964 | On the Crystal Problem, Part 15 | crystal | 789 |
| Ashby1966 | On the Lens Problem, Part 17 | lens | 774 |
| Gisler1968 | On the Mirror Problem, Part 19 | mirror | 784 |
| Elling1970 | On the Fibre Problem, Part 21 | fibre | 779 |
| Castell1972 | On the Crystal Problem, Part 23 | crystal | 789 |

**Grouped by apparatus:**
- **Lens** (Ashby): Ashby1950, Ashby1958, Ashby1966
- **Mirror** (Gisler): Gisler1952, Gisler1960, Gisler1968
- **Fibre** (Elling): Elling1954, Elling1962, Elling1970
- **Crystal** (Castell): Castell1956, Castell1964, Castell1972

Limit: the 300-character cap meant I did not see the remaining 474 to 489 characters of any abstract. The visible part only repeats the one sentence, so the rest probably does too, but I have not confirmed it.

review.notes: Pages the selection with --limit 5 --max-chars 300 to completion via cursors; each of the 12 keys read once, in order. Discloses that every abstract was cut (774-789 characters) and that the unseen remainder is unconfirmed. Titles, lengths and the repeated sentence match the responses. Borderline: the per-apparatus grouping labels groups by key prefix ('Lens (Ashby)'); authors were not selected, but the label is read as the key prefix rather than counted as a claim.
